profile.audience: people who just moved out for the first time
profile.cta: save this for your next grocery run

research_material:

every recipe assumes I already know what a roux is

pain_points: Don't know how to cook rice without specialized equipment
Recipes assume prior cooking knowledge (like what a roux is)
Feeling lost when recipes use unexplained culinary terms
Lack of confidence in basic cooking techniques
Fear of failing at foundational cooking skills

hooks.text: Most people mess up rice. Here's exactly why.
Your phone timer is about to save dinner.
What's the one thing nobody tells you about rice?
Perfect rice every single time. No exceptions.
Rice doesn't have to be scary or mushy.
Burnt rice? Crunchy rice? We're fixing this today.
If your rice turned out bad, this is why.
You've been eyeballing the water. Stop.
Watch me make rice without touching it once.
The pot matters more than you think.

winner.text: You've been eyeballing the water. Stop.
winner.reasoning: This directly calls out the exact mistake first-time cooks make, uses the warm 'you' voice, and creates immediate curiosity about the right method. For someone newly independent, it validates their struggle while positioning the video as the helpful solution they didn't know they needed.

runner_up.text: Your phone timer is about to save dinner.
runner_up.reasoning: Relatable and encouraging without shame. Uses familiar tool (phone) to demystify cooking, appeals to beginners' desire for a safety net, and the word 'save' emotionally resonates with someone anxious about cooking for themselves.

script.script:
[HOOK - 0-3 sec]

[ON-SCREEN TEXT: You've been eyeballing the water. Stop.]

Voiceover: Yeah, I see you standing in the pasta aisle wondering if you need to buy *another* thing.

[PAUSE]

[CUT]

[PROBLEM]

Voiceover: Here's the thing — tap water works just fine for cooking pasta, rice, and vegetables. You don't need fancy bottled water.

[ON-SCREEN TEXT: Save your money.]

[CUT]

[VALUE]

Voiceover: Use tap water. It's the same stuff that comes out of your kitchen sink. Same water restaurants use. Same water your parents used.

The only exception? If your tap water tastes *really* off, a cheap filter pitcher does the job.

[ON-SCREEN TEXT: One less thing to buy.]

[PAUSE]

[CUT]

[CTA]

Voiceover: Save this for your next grocery run so you remember — skip the water aisle and put those dollars toward actual ingredients.

[ON-SCREEN TEXT: You've got this.]
script.viewer_takeaway: Tap water is fine for cooking; bottled water is an unnecessary expense for new home cooks, freeing up budget for real groceries.

justifications.clarity: Hook + problem statement land instantly; 'tap water works' eliminates confusion in first 5 seconds.
justifications.retention: Value section reassures but lacks a surprising angle—permission to skip feels expected rather than rewarding.
justifications.save_potential: Practical grocery-aisle trigger makes it bookmarkable, but the insight isn't novel enough to feel like essential reference material.
justifications.shareability: Relatable scenario but lacks humor, controversy, or emotional punch that drives tagging friends or DM forwarding.
justifications.audience_fit: Perfectly addresses first-time mover anxiety about 'doing it right'—directly solves a real budget + confidence gap.
justifications.cta_strength: Clear, specific, low-friction ask tied to a real moment (next grocery run); save-for-reference is natural for this niche.

weaknesses.issue: Middle section (slides 2–4) lacks a compelling reason to stay—reassurance alone doesn't generate scroll-stopping retention.
weaknesses.fix: Add a small cost angle in voiceover: 'A case of bottled water? That's $5–8 a month. Over a year, that's money you could spend on actual ingredients like good olive oil or fresh herbs.' This quantifies the benefit and makes the choice feel financially smart, not just acceptable.

weaknesses.issue: Shareability is weak because the post doesn't create a 'that's me' moment—it's advice, not validation or humor.
weaknesses.fix: Rewrite hook voiceover: 'I used to stand in the pasta aisle thinking I was *supposed* to buy fancy water. Turns out, I was just broke and scared of doing it wrong.' This self-deprecating admission makes first-time movers feel seen and more likely to tag a friend moving out.

weaknesses.issue: The filter pitcher exception (slide 4) feels tacked on and dilutes the core message—it introduces a product consideration when the whole point is to *avoid* unnecessary purchases.
weaknesses.fix: Remove the filter pitcher slide or reposition it as a last-resort mention in voiceover only: 'If your tap water tastes genuinely bad—like, undrinkable bad—a cheap $10 filter pitcher is a one-time buy, not a weekly grocery habit.' Keep the visual focus on tap water confidence, not alternative purchases.

captions: stop pretending you need fancy water for pasta. your tap is fine, your budget will thank you, and your next grocery trip just got cheaper. save this for the pasta aisle 👇
first time cooking for yourself? tap water works. seriously. skip the water aisle, spend those dollars on ingredients that actually matter. save this for your next grocery run 💚
growth.final_call_reason: Strong audience fit and clarity, but retention and shareability lag because it's advice without emotional hook—weaving in relatable self-doubt and quantified savings will lift engagement and make it worth the production cost.
